text.title: Diary Study Basics Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for specifying a diary study before it runs: declaring the trigger design of each entry template, capping per-entry cost, sizing duration to the behaviour cycle, putting reminders on the entry channel, setting a compliance threshold with over-recruitment, and anchoring the exit interview to the participant's own entries.

rule.statement: Each template in `entry_templates` MUST declare its trigger design: interval-contingent (fixed cadence, e.g. end of day), signal-contingent (prompted at random or scheduled times), or event-contingent (fires on a named observable event the participant can recognise, e.g. "every time you check the balance"). The named event MUST be written in the participant's words in the template.

rationale.source: Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli, "Diary Methods: Capturing Life as It Is Lived" (Annual Review of Psychology, 2003)

rule.rationale: The three designs answer different questions and cannot be substituted. Interval entries yield even coverage but summarise the day away; event entries yield in-the-moment detail but are blind to non-events — the times the person wanted to act and did not. A study asking how often something happens needs event triggers or it measures diligence.

rule.statement: A single entry MUST be completable in under about three minutes on the participant's phone; the spec MUST state the field count and include at least one open free-text field. Templates over roughly 8-10 fields per entry are rejected or split across entry types.

rationale.source: Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli (2003) — participant burden and compliance decay

rule.rationale: Compliance falls with per-entry burden and falls again with study length, and it does not fail loudly: a heavy template yields two thorough days followed by a fortnight of one-word entries. Those entries pass every completeness check and contain nothing, so burden shows up as noise, never as a missing-data warning.

rule.statement: Study length MUST cover at least two full cycles of the behaviour under study — daily behaviour: 1-2 weeks; weekly cycle (payroll, sprint, shopping run): 3+ weeks; monthly cycle (billing, rent, reporting): 2+ months — and the spec MUST name the cycle it is sizing against. The first 1-2 days MUST be marked as a novelty window in the analysis plan.

rationale.source: Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli (2003) — reactivity and study duration; NN/g diary-study guidance

rule.rationale: One cycle cannot distinguish a routine from a one-off, and participants are measurably more diligent and more reflective in the first days because they are performing the study. A study shorter than the novelty window measures the effect of being observed rather than the behaviour.

rule.statement: Every row of `reminder_schedule` MUST use the same device and app the entry is submitted in (push in the capture app, or SMS/WhatsApp linking straight into the form), MUST be timed to just after the expected trigger moment, and MUST NOT exceed one reminder per expected entry.

rationale.source: Experience-sampling practice (Larson & Csikszentmihalyi, ESM) applied to mobile capture

rule.rationale: Each channel switch between reminder and form is an abandonment point — the participant reads the email, intends to fill the form later, and later never has the context. Over-reminding produces the opposite failure: participants mute notifications, which removes the prompt permanently and looks identical to disengagement.

rule.statement: `compliance_threshold` MUST state the minimum share of expected entries for a participant to count as complete (commonly around 70%), the remediation step when a participant falls below it, and the recruitment margin — recruit above target headcount to absorb attrition. Participants below threshold MUST be reported as excluded with a count, not removed silently.

rationale.source: Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli (2003) — attrition and selective compliance

rule.rationale: Diary attrition is non-random: the people who drop out are the people the product fits worst or who are busiest, exactly the segment of interest. Quietly analysing only the compliant participants leaves a sample of the most engaged users and a report that says the product works.

rule.statement: `exit_interview_hook` MUST commit to opening from the participant's own entries — specific entries quoted back with their timestamps — and the debrief MUST be scheduled within a few days of the final entry. Generic debrief prompts ("how did you find it?") as the anchor are rejected.

rationale.source: Diary + exit-interview practice (NN/g diary-study method; Bolger et al. on retrospective recall)

rule.rationale: Diary entries are terse by design, and their meaning decays with the same recall curve the diary was built to defeat. Quoting the entry back while it is still recallable recovers the context; a generic debrief a fortnight later collects a fresh summary opinion and discards the study's main asset.

rule.statement: Skip when (a) the behaviour occurs less than about twice per week — the study window needed exceeds any realistic incentive budget; (b) the question is answerable from instrumentation you already ship, since telemetry beats self-report on counts; (c) the behaviour happens in a single sitting you could simply observe — use contextual inquiry; (d) no incentive and no dedicated capture channel exist, since compliance is bought, not requested.

rationale.source: Methodology preconditions for longitudinal self-report (Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli, 2003)

rule.rationale: A diary study spends weeks of participant goodwill before producing any data. Run on a behaviour too rare or already instrumented, it returns a thin, mostly-empty corpus after the point where switching methods was still cheap.
